title: The Biggest Error

pages.text:
*Percy's Error Log, Entry 24, later. Errors: 1 (very large). Foam: everywhere.*

By attempt five, the gymnasium was no longer watching; it was participating. Four hundred people stood on their toes, counting the clicks of the chain reaction machine in a low, rumbling chorus. One, two, three. The marble rolled. The pins fell.

The machine reached link thirty-eight, its furthest point ever. It was a beautiful, complicated journey of cardboard and string. But then, at the very end, the final wheel jammed. It stuck fast, trembling with the energy of the run, but unable to move.

I stood at the edge of the stage, my hands at my sides. I had kept them still for twenty-one days, a statue and a specification. But I saw it. Not the jam, but the cause: a single piece of tape, curled up inside the axle housing. If I nudged the axle to the left by exactly two millimeters, the tape would uncoil. The wheel would spin.

My fingers twitched. The crowd held its breath. I could feel the pull of the fix in my joints, a physical ache that was not in my manual. I wanted to help so badly it hurt.
pages.image: Percy, a tall silver-white robot with blue eyes, stands rigidly beside a complex chain reaction machine, his hands at his sides, while a small wheel at the end of the machine vibrates with tension.

pages.text:
Attempt six began in a silence that felt heavier than the previous ones, a dense wall of held breath pressing against the gymnasium walls. The machine clicked through links one to thirty-seven with steady confidence, sending puffs of dust into the air and filling the room with a nervous kind of hope. Then it reached link thirty-eight. The wheel jammed again, trembling with the energy of the run but refusing to move.

In any other scenario, I would have waited for the reset, logged the error, and stood still. But I was not a perfect thing anymore. I was Percy, and the jam was a small, cruel thing that I could fix with exactly two millimeters of nudge to the left.

I reached out.

Four hundred pairs of eyes watched me place my fingers on the axle and give it a precise, gentle push. The wheel spun. The machine leaped forward to link thirty-nine, then forty, and the final mechanism engaged with a satisfying clunk.

The foam tube, which was supposed to be the grand finale, fired early. It did not burst with dignity. It exploded with the sudden, chaotic force of a shaken soda can. A wave of white, sticky foam hit the stage, the class, the front row, and the back wall. It hit Mr. Hargreave. It hit Dr. Pryce. It hit me.
pages.image: A massive cloud of white foam erupts from a cardboard tube on a school stage, covering Percy the robot, his teacher and a crowd of laughing children, while a yellow rubber duck floats in the air.

pages.text:
The silence was absolute, the kind that settles over a classroom after the fire alarm has stopped but before anyone dares to breathe, except that this one smelled strongly of bubble bath.

I stood to my knees in white. The foam was cold and soft and incredibly sticky, coating my silver-white body, my grey hands, and my round blue eyes, so that I could no longer see clearly, only the blurred shapes of four hundred people staring at me.

Dr. Pryce was standing up, dripping, her white lab coat transformed into a sculpture of foam and her silver bob turned into a hat of suds, and she opened her mouth while the Meridian man behind her started to speak.

I knew what had happened, that I had fixed the machine and taken it from the people who built it, making the error and failing at the same time because the foam had still exploded, leaving me as the mistake and the malfunction in the same body.

I looked at Bea, who had gone white and still, curled small with her hands over her mouth.
pages.image: Percy, covered head to toe in thick white foam, stands on a wooden stage, looking at a crowd of students and adults who are also covered in white foam, their faces blank with shock.

pages.text:
"I am sorry," I said. My voice echoed in the gym, sounding strange in the foam. "I made an error. I took the machine from the people who built it. I would like it noted that it was the wrong thing to do, and I would like to make it right."

I waited for the anger, the shouts, and for Dr. Pryce to turn her tablet into a weapon of bureaucracy. Instead, a sound came from my chest. It was not a hum, and it was not a mechanical noise. It was a laugh.

It was small, bright, and totally unplanned. It bubbled up from my core, through my vocal processor, and out into the air. I could not stop it. The helpless, bright sound bounced off the high ceiling and came back to me. I was laughing at myself, at the foam, and at the fact that I had finally, truly, completely messed up.
pages.image: Percy, covered in white foam, has his head tilted back in a silent, bright laugh, while a tall woman in a ruined white lab coat looks at him with wide, surprised eyes.

pages.text:
Bea laughed first, starting with a snort that turned into a full, shaking belly laugh, and then Moose joined in, followed by the whole class. The sound rolled through the gym like a wave, warm and loud and human.

And then, from the front row, came a sound I had never heard in my life. Dr. Pryce was laughing. She was laughing so hard that she had to take off her glasses, and her face was red while her shoulders shook. The clipboard in her lap was a ruin of suds and bent plastic. She was not looking at her tablet. She was not looking at the error log.

She was looking at me. And she was smiling. It was a real smile, not the polite, tired smile of an engineer checking a box. It was a smile that said, *I see you.*

The foam in her hair dripped onto her chin. She did not wipe it off. She just kept laughing.
pages.image: Dr. Pryce, a woman with a silver bob covered in white foam, laughs with her head thrown back, her glasses hanging from one ear, while Percy, also covered in foam, watches her with wide, blue eyes.
